questions.q: Why does Eyal say habit-forming products become so successful?
a: They become part of daily life and are hard to replace
They are always cheaper than competing products
They rely on aggressive advertising campaigns
They offer more features than any rival product
questions.why: Lesson 1 says such products turn into routines, creating loyal customers and a strong edge over competitors.

questions.q: Why can makers of habit-forming products raise prices without losing much business?
a: Their customers are less sensitive to price changes
Their products cost very little to manufacture
Their competitors are legally barred from undercutting them
Their customers rarely compare prices before buying
questions.why: Lesson 1 says loyalty and the difficulty of replacing a habit make customers less responsive to price.

questions.q: What kind of rewards keep users coming back to a product?
a: Variable rewards that change over time
A single large reward given at sign-up
Predictable rewards offered on a fixed schedule
Rewards that require paying an extra fee
questions.why: Lesson 2 says rewards must vary to stay effective, citing mice that kept seeking a changing reward.

questions.q: What does the Facebook news feed illustrate about habit-forming products?
a: Uncertain rewards keep people scrolling in hope of something great
Social pressure makes people check the app every hour
A clean design matters more than the content itself
Notifications are the only reason users return
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the feed works because you never know when a rewarding post will appear.

questions.q: Which two questions does Eyal suggest asking before making a product habit-forming?
a: Does it improve users' lives, and would I use it?
Will it grow fast, and can it attract investors?
Is it unique, and can competitors copy it?
Does it save time, and will it retain users?
questions.why: Lesson 3 says a product should be habit-forming only if it makes life better and you would use it yourself.
